The queen triggerfish Balistes vetula attains a maximum total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], measured from the tip of the snout to the end of the caudal fin, as determined from extensive surveys of the artisanal catch throughout the Caribbean, a size that rivals the largest recorded for the Balistidae in the Atlantic and reflects the species' capacity to exploit abundant hard-shelled prey. This species demonstrates a robust, somewhat compressed body form typical of the Balistidae and can reach large sizes relative to many reef-dwelling teleosts. Based on studies of size at first reproduction in related species within the genus Balistes, particularly Balistes capriscus, the total length at puberty has been estimated at 23.5 centimeters [Lp = 23.5 centimeters]. This value is considered a reliable proxy for the onset of gonadal development, though direct histological validation for B. vetula remains limited. The attainment of this length marks a critical transition from the juvenile to the sub-adult phase, during which individuals begin to invest energy into reproductive structures. Observations of captive individuals held at the Instituto de Ciencias del Mar laboratories indicate that growth to this size can occur remarkably quickly under optimal feeding regimes.

At the time of hatching, emerging yolk-sac larvae are minuscule, with an estimated wet weight at birth of just 0.000195 grams [Wwb = 0.000195 grams]. This remarkably low initial mass is extrapolated from the egg diameter of approximately 0.62 millimeters documented for the congener Balistes capriscus, whose eggs are broadly comparable in size. Field-collectors noted that after a 48-hour incubation period at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the chorion ruptures and a transparent prolarva emerges, still heavily dependent on its endogenous yolk supply. The tiny size of these newly hatched individuals reflects the pelagic, energetically inexpensive egg strategy typical of many coastal balistids. Despite their minuscule mass, these alevins possess fully developed pectoral fins and are able to swim weakly within hours of eclosion. Survival during this lecithotrophic stage is critically dependent on warm, stable water temperatures to ensure rapid yolk absorption and timely onset of exogenous feeding.

When maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum lifespan observed for queen triggerfish in captivity has been recorded at 13 years [am = 13 years]. This longevity was documented in a long-term holding study at the Bermuda Aquarium, Museum and Zoo, where a single individual survived for that duration before succumbing to age-related physiological deterioration. Another specimen kept at the same facility, but under a slightly cooler temperature regime, died at 11 years, underscoring the modulating effect of temperature on aging rates in tropical fishes. The species is considered relatively long-lived compared to many other Caribbean reef fishes, likely a consequence of its robust body armor and a diet that reduces predation risk. Senescent individuals often show reduced feeding activity, a loss of body condition, and a characteristic fraying of the dorsal and anal fin rays prior to natural mortality.

As a spawning adult, the queen triggerfish exhibits a moderately high reproductive output that is constrained by environmental temperature. Field fecundity estimates based on tank-based trials in Brazil suggest that females can produce approximately 800,000 eggs annually, with each reproductive event yielding roughly 2,192 eggs at a stable thermal environment of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The frequency of spawning events is approximately one per year, a pattern common among broadcast spawners that compensates for substantial egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment.

The plateau in body mass at 5,400 grams [Wwi = 5,400 grams] suggests an energetic ceiling imposed by the species' diet of calcareous invertebrates. This substantial mass, achieved relatively late in life and correlated with a total length approaching 60 centimeters, indicates a robust body shape. Comparative morphometric data from across its range, including the Bahamas and the Gulf of Mexico, suggest that this asymptotic mass may represent an upper physiological limit for the species, likely constrained by the energetic demands of a diet consisting primarily of hard-shelled benthic invertebrates. The thick, leathery skin and powerful jaw musculature necessary to crush molluscan prey represent significant investments in somatic tissue that contribute to this ultimate body weight. Field studies have noted that the heaviest individuals are almost invariably female, possibly reflecting the energetic requirements of vitellogenesis and the capacity of the abdominal cavity to accommodate large gonad masses. This sexual dimorphism in ultimate size warrants further investigation.
